summary: This unit teaches the geometry a fabricator uses every day: the names of lines, angles, shapes and solids, the sums for circumferences, cone sectors and sheet sizes, and the compass-and-rule constructions for right angles, hexagons, octagons and divided circles. You will learn to develop flat patterns for cylinders, pipes cut at an angle, cones, frustums and pyramids by the parallel line and radial line methods, add allowances, then mark out, cut, form and check the job.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). Much fabrication starts as a flat sheet that is cut to a **pattern** and then rolled, folded or bent into shape: a round duct, a hopper, a funnel, a cone-shaped hood, a pipe that meets a sloping roof, a tray. If the pattern is wrong, the job will not close, will not fit, or will be the wrong size, and the steel is wasted.

This unit teaches you to **develop basic geometric shapes**: to use the geometry and simple sums behind patterns, construct accurate shapes with compass, dividers and rule, and develop, mark out, cut and form simple patterns in sheet metal. In Jamaican shops this is the skill behind extractor hoods for restaurants and jerk pans, ducting, chutes and hoppers for farms and factories, water-tank shells, funnels, gutters and pipe bends.
**Who it is for:** Welding Level 2 trainees. You need to be able to measure accurately and use a calculator for simple sums.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Work safely with sheet and marking tools
Handle sharp sheet, snips, scribers, guillotines and rolls without injury.
Choose and use rule, square, protractor, scriber, dividers, trammels, odd-leg callipers, punches and marking fluid.
Name lines, angles, triangles, polygons, the parts of a circle and the common solids.
Work out circumferences, mean diameters, stretch-outs, cone sector angles, true lengths and sheet sizes, and check them.
Bisect lines and angles; construct 90°, 60°, 45° and 30°; draw hexagons, octagons and triangles; divide circles and lines into equal parts; find a lost centre.
Develop cylinders, pipes cut at an angle, cones, frustums and pyramids by the parallel line and radial line methods.
Add lap, seam, wired edge, safe edge and flange allowances where the drawing asks.
Test the pattern in card, mark it on sheet, cut and deburr it, roll or fold it, and check the job against the drawing.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on tools, shapes and terms, constructions, calculations, true lengths, pattern development and checking.
A **written paper** with short answers (terms and simple sums) and essays describing constructions and developments step by step.

**Practical tasks**: constructing and cutting out shapes (hexagon, octagon, triangle, divided disc, angles) in 0.8 mm sheet; and developing, making and checking a pipe cut at 45° (parallel line method) and a cone frustum (radial line method).

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, and write down your working. In the exam, a correct method with a slip in the sum still shows the assessor what you know; on the job, a checked sum saves a sheet of steel.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Sheet edges, burrs and offcuts cut like knives. Wear **gloves** when handling and cutting sheet, and deburr edges straight away.
Wear **safety glasses** when cutting, drilling, filing and riveting.
Keep the hand that holds the sheet well away from snip blades and guillotine blades. Use the guillotine only with its guards in place, one person operating it.
At the bending rolls, keep fingers, loose gloves and sleeves well clear of the rolls: they pull in anything they grip.
Put offcuts straight into the scrap bin; never leave them on the floor or bench.
Keep scribers, dividers and trammel points pointing down on the bench, or with a cover on the point, when not in use. Never carry them in a pocket.

head: Tool
Used for
rows: Measuring and marking straight lines; a long straight edge for long lines
Marking and checking lines at 90° (and 45° with a combination square) to a straight edge
Measuring and marking angles such as 30°, 45° or 120°, and checking constructed angles
Scratching fine, lasting lines on metal, for cut lines
Bend lines and lines on coated sheet: a scratch on a bend line can crack when it is bent, and a scratch through galvanising lets rust start
Stepping off equal distances, transferring sizes and scribing small arcs and circles
Drawing arcs and circles on paper and card
Scribing large arcs and circles that are too big for dividers: two points on a long bar
One curved leg and one pointed leg: scribing lines parallel to an edge
Centre punch: marking hole and arc centres so dividers and drills do not slip. Dot punch: light dots along a line so it can still be seen after cutting
Painted on bright steel so scribed lines show up clearly
A true, flat surface to support the sheet while marking
Drawing 30°, 45°, 60° and 90° lines and scaled drawings on paper

blocks.p: A **datum** is the fixed straight edge or line that all measurements start from. Before marking out, check that one edge of the sheet is truly straight (with a straight edge) and use it as the datum, or scribe a datum line. Measure every size from the datum, not from the last mark, so small errors do not add up.

flow: Read the drawing; check the sizes and work out any sums
Check and choose a straight datum edge, or scribe a datum line
Paint marking fluid on the area to be marked, and let it dry
Mark the main lines from the datum with rule, square and scriber
Punch centres lightly, then scribe arcs and circles with dividers or trammels
Mark bend lines in pencil or fine marker
Check every size against the drawing before the first cut

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet
At 90° (a right angle) to another line

head: Triangle
What it has
rows: All three sides equal and all three angles 60°
Two equal sides, and the two angles opposite them equal
One angle of 90°. The longest side, opposite the right angle, is the **hypotenuse**

blocks.p: The three inside angles of **any triangle add up to 180°**. In a right-angled triangle, Pythagoras' rule links the sides: hypotenuse² = side² + other side². A triangle with sides 3, 4 and 5 (or 30, 40 and 50, or 300, 400 and 500) always has a right angle.

head: Shape
What it has
rows: Four equal sides, four right angles
Opposite sides equal, four right angles
Four equal sides; opposite sides parallel; no right angles
Opposite sides equal and parallel; no right angles
A flat shape with all sides equal and all angles equal

blocks.p: The inside angles of any four-sided shape add up to **360°**. For any polygon with n sides, they add up to (n − 2) × 180°.

head: Part
Meaning
rows: The point in the middle, the same distance from every point on the edge
The distance from the centre to the edge
The distance across the circle through its centre: twice the radius
The distance all the way round the circle
A straight line joining two points on the circle; the diameter is the longest chord
Part of the curved edge of a circle
A slice of a circle between two radii and an arc, like a slice of pie
The part of a circle cut off by a chord
A quarter and a half of a circle
A straight line that touches the circle at one point only; it is always at 90° to the radius at that point

head: Solid
Description
Pattern method
rows: Two equal flat ends joined by flat sides, such as a square or rectangular duct
Two equal circular ends joined by a curved surface: a pipe or tank
A flat circular base rising to a point (the **apex**) directly above its centre
A flat base with straight edges, rising to an apex
A cone or pyramid with its top cut off parallel to the base, such as a hopper
A ball: it cannot be made from one flat sheet

blocks.p: Use π (pi) = **3.142**, or the π key on your calculator; the answers differ only slightly (a few tenths of a millimetre on most jobs). Use the one your instructor or the exam question gives. Write down each step, and work every sum twice.

When plate is rolled, the outside of the bend stretches and the inside is squeezed. Only the middle of the thickness stays the same length. So the length of plate for a cylinder is worked out from the **mean diameter**, half-way through the plate.

head: Drawing gives
Mean diameter
Example
rows: OD 320 mm, 4 mm plate: 320 − 4 = 316 mm, length 3.142 × 316 = 992.9 mm

blocks.note: On thin sheet (under about 1 mm) the difference is small, and many jobs simply use the drawing diameter. On plate it matters: the wrong diameter makes the shell too big or too small by several millimetres. Always check whether the drawing gives the inside or the outside diameter.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Rectangular duct:** the length of sheet to go once round is the perimeter: 2 × (width + height). A 400 mm × 250 mm duct needs 2 × 650 = 1 300 mm, plus any seam allowance.

**Open-top box from one sheet:** add the depth twice to each side. A box 300 mm long, 150 mm wide and 80 mm deep needs a sheet (300 + 160) × (150 + 160) = 460 mm × 310 mm, with an 80 mm square cut from each corner, before allowances.

**How many pieces from a sheet:** divide each side of the sheet by the piece size and take the whole numbers only, then multiply. Try the pieces both ways round. A 2 440 mm × 1 220 mm sheet gives 4 × 3 = 12 pieces of 600 mm × 400 mm (or 6 × 2 = 12 turned the other way), if no allowance is made for cutting.

blocks.p: The pattern for a cone is a **sector** of a circle. Its radius is the cone's **slant height** (from the apex to the edge of the base), and its curved edge must equal the circumference of the base.

head: Step
Example: cone with base diameter 180 mm and vertical height 120 mm
rows: Sector angle = base radius ÷ slant height × 360°

blocks.h: True length of a sloping edge

blocks.p: The true length of a sloping line is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle. One side is its **vertical height**; the other is its **length seen in the plan**.

head: Example: square pyramid, base sides 200 mm, vertical height 300 mm
Working
rows: Plan length of a corner edge (centre to corner)
True length of the sloping edge

blocks.note: Units: work in millimetres throughout. 1 m = 1 000 mm. Round only at the end, and to the nearest 0.5 mm or 1 mm for marking out.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Constructions use only a **compass (or dividers) and a straight edge**. They are more accurate than a protractor on large work, and they work on steel as well as on paper. Leave the construction lines visible, so your work can be checked.

flow: Open the compass to a little **more than half** the length of the line AB
With the point on A, draw an arc above and below the line
With the same opening and the point on B, draw arcs that cross the first two
Join the two crossing points: this line cuts AB exactly in half and is **perpendicular** (at 90°) to it
With the compass point on the corner, draw an arc cutting both arms
From each of those two points, with the same radius, draw arcs that cross inside the angle
Draw a line from the corner through the crossing point: it splits the angle into two equal angles

head: Angle
How
rows: 90° at a point P on a line
Arc from P cutting the line on both sides; from those two points, wider arcs that cross above the line; join P to the crossing
90° at the end of a line
Use the 3-4-5 rule: mark 3 units along the line and 4 units up, and adjust until the diagonal is 5 units
Arc from P cutting the line; with the **same radius**, put the point where the arc cuts the line and mark the arc again; join P to this mark
Step the same radius twice along the arc from the line (60° + 60°)

ul: **A parallel line:** from two points well apart on the line, draw arcs of the same radius; draw a line touching the tops of both arcs. On sheet with a straight edge, use odd-leg callipers.

**Dividing a line into equal parts** (say 7): from one end draw a sloping line at any angle; step off 7 equal spaces along it with dividers; join the last mark to the other end of the line; draw lines parallel to this through each mark. They cut the line into 7 equal parts.

head: Construction
How
Check
rows: Draw the base s; from each end swing an arc of radius s; join the ends to the crossing point
Draw a circle of radius s; from any point on it, step the radius round the circle: it fits exactly **six** times; join the marks
Sides all s; across the corners 2 × s; each inside angle 120°. If the last step does not land on the start, the compass has slipped: start again
Draw the diagonals to find the centre; from each corner, swing an arc **through the centre** (radius = half the diagonal) to cut the two sides; join the eight points
Eight equal sides; each inside angle 135°
Step the radius round the circle to get 6 points; bisect each of the six spaces to get 12
Spaces equal when stepped with dividers
Draw two diameters at 90°; bisect the right angles for 8
Draw two chords well apart; bisect each one; the bisectors cross at the centre
Every point on the circle the same distance from it
Tangent at a point on a circle
Draw the radius to the point; construct a line at 90° to the radius there
Touches the circle at one point only

blocks.note: For a regular octagon in a 100 mm square, the arcs have a radius of half the diagonal: √(100² + 100²) ÷ 2 = 70.7 mm, and each side of the octagon comes out at about 41.4 mm.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: On a large sheet, a rectangle is truly square when its **two diagonals are equal**. A corner can be checked or set with the 3-4-5 rule: 300 mm along one edge and 400 mm along the other should be exactly 500 mm apart.
Patterns are developed from drawings of the job in two or more views, drawn full size (or to scale) on paper. This is called **orthographic projection**.

head: View
What it shows
rows: The job seen from the front: heights and widths
The job seen from directly above: lengths and widths, and the shape of round parts as circles
The job seen from the side

blocks.p: The views are lined up with each other, so a point can be **projected** (carried across with a square or set square) from one view to another. The drawing carries a symbol that tells you which way the views are arranged; ask your instructor if you are unsure.

A line shows at its **true length** only when it is parallel to the view you are looking at. A line that slopes away from you looks shorter than it really is. On a cone, the sloping side seen at the edge of the elevation is a true length; the sloping corner edges of a pyramid are not, because they slope away from you.

ul: **By calculation:** true length = √(plan length² + vertical height²).
**By drawing:** draw a right angle; mark the vertical height on one side and the plan length on the other; the line joining them is the true length.
**By rotating:** in the plan, swing the line round about its foot until it is parallel to the elevation, then project it up; it now shows at true length.

blocks.note: Patterns must be drawn with true lengths. Measuring a sloping edge straight off the elevation of a pyramid gives a pattern that is too small and will not close.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Pattern development: the parallel line method

blocks.p: A **development** (or pattern) is the flat shape that, when cut out and rolled or folded, forms the solid. The **parallel line method** is used for shapes whose sides are parallel lines: **prisms, cylinders and pipes**, including pipes cut off at an angle.
The pattern is a rectangle. Its height is the height of the cylinder; its length, the **stretch-out**, is the circumference (π × diameter, or π × mean diameter for plate), plus any seam allowance.

blocks.h: A pipe cut off at an angle (truncated cylinder)

flow: Draw the elevation of the pipe with the sloping cut at the top, and the plan below it: a circle of the pipe's diameter
Divide the plan circle into **12 equal parts** and number the points, starting at the seam
Project each point up into the elevation, giving 12 lines along the pipe, each ending at the sloping cut
Beside the elevation, draw the **stretch-out line** equal to the circumference, and divide it into the same 12 equal parts, numbered in the same order
Draw a line up from each division
From each point where a line meets the cut in the elevation, project across to the line with the same number on the pattern
Join the points with a **smooth curve** (a flexible strip helps), never straight lines between them
Add the seam allowance, then cut the pattern in card, roll it and check it against the drawing

blocks.p: Put the seam on the **shortest line**, so the seam to be joined is as short as possible.

head: Example: pipe 120 mm diameter cut at 45°, shortest side 60 mm
Values
rows: 60 + 120 = 180 mm (a 45° cut across a 120 mm pipe rises by 120 mm)

blocks.note: The more divisions, the smoother and more accurate the curve. Twelve is usual for small pipes; use 16 or 24 for large ones.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Two-piece 90° elbow:** two pipes, each cut at 45°, joined. The two patterns can be marked from one sheet with a single shared curve, saving metal.

**Lobster-back (segmented) bend:** several short pieces of pipe, each cut at an angle and joined to make a bend. The bend is shared equally between the joints; the two end pieces are half the length of the middle ones.
**Rectangular duct (prism):** stretch-out = perimeter; the corners are fold lines, marked in pencil.

sections.title: Pattern development: the radial line method

blocks.p: The **radial line method** is used for shapes whose sloping lines all meet at one point, the **apex**: **right cones, pyramids and their frustums**. The pattern is drawn with lines radiating from the apex.

flow: Draw the elevation of the cone; its sloping side is the true **slant height**
With the slant height as radius, draw an arc from a point that will be the apex

Step the circumference of the base along the arc: divide the plan circle into 12 and step those 12 spaces along the arc with dividers, or mark the sector angle (base radius ÷ slant height × 360°) with a protractor
Join both ends of the arc to the apex: the sector is the pattern
Add the seam allowance and check the pattern in card

blocks.note: A divider step is a straight chord, which is a little shorter than the arc it spans. Twelve steps come out about 1% short, so on a large cone use more divisions, or work out the sector angle and the arc length instead.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: A frustum of a cone (a hopper)

flow: Draw the elevation full size or to scale: top and bottom diameters and the vertical height
**Extend the two sloping sides upward until they meet**: this is the apex of the full cone
From the apex, draw one arc with a radius to the **bottom** edge and one with a radius to the **top** edge
Make the outer arc equal to the base circumference, by stepping the divisions or by the sector angle (base radius ÷ slant height of the full cone × 360°)
Draw lines from the apex through the ends of the outer arc: the shape between the two arcs and the two lines is the pattern
Add the seam allowance; check in card

head: Frustum example
Working
rows: Bottom diameter 300 mm, top diameter 150 mm, vertical height 200 mm
The radius halves over 200 mm, so the apex is another 200 mm up: 400 mm in all
Slant height to the bottom edge
Slant height to the top edge

flow: Draw the elevation and plan; find the **true length of a sloping corner edge** (see Views and true lengths)
With the true length as radius, draw an arc from the apex point
Step the length of one base side along the arc four times, as chords
Join the points to each other with straight lines and to the apex: four triangles make the pattern
Add allowances; fold lines in pencil

blocks.p: For a **frustum of a pyramid**, draw a second arc with the true length to the top edge, and join the points on it in the same way.

Shapes that are neither parallel nor radial, such as a **transition piece** (square at one end, round at the other), are developed by **triangulation**: the surface is split into triangles and each is drawn at its true size. You will meet it in later units.

An allowance is **extra metal** added to a pattern so the edges can be joined, stiffened or made safe. Without it the finished job would be too small or could not be joined. The size depends on the joint and the sheet thickness: take it from the drawing or the Centre's tables.

head: Allowance
What it is for
Typical size (follow the drawing)
rows: One edge overlaps the other, for riveting, spot welding, soldering or a lap weld
The width of the overlap, on one edge only (for example 10 mm)
Both edges folded, hooked together and locked flat
About three times the width of the finished seam in total, shared between the two edges
An open edge rolled round a wire: stiff, and no sharp edge
An edge folded back flat: stiff and safe to handle
An edge turned out to bolt or join to another part
The flange width on the drawing
None, or as the weld gap needs

blocks.note: Put each allowance on the right edge. A lap added to both ends makes a cylinder one lap too big.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Check the paper or card pattern against the drawing; test it by rolling or folding the card
Lay the sheet flat; place the pattern close to an edge, or fit several together, to waste as little metal as possible
**Clamp or weight** the pattern so it cannot move
Scribe round it on the cut lines; mark bend lines in pencil; punch hole centres
Check the marked-out sheet against the drawing before the first cut

head: Tool
Use
rows: Straight lines and gentle curves in thin sheet
Curves and circles; on many, the handle colour shows the cut: yellow straight, red left-hand, green right-hand
Long straight cuts, quickly and square
Thicker sheet and complicated shapes, as the Centre allows

ul: Cut on the waste side, just outside the line, so the pattern is not undersize.
**Deburr** every edge with a file or deburring tool, to remove the sharp edge and finish to the line.
Roll cylinders and cones in the bending rolls a little at a time, checking the curve with a template, until the edges meet. Without rolls, form thin sheet round a pipe or stake.
Cones roll with the small end moving more slowly than the large end: feed carefully and check often.
Fold boxes and ducts on the folding machine along the pencilled bend lines.
Join the seam as the drawing says: rivets, lock seam, solder, spot weld or weld.
Measure the diameter **across several places and in different directions** along the length, not once at one end.
Check the height, the angle of any cut, and the size of each opening.
Check the seam meets evenly along its whole length, with no gap or step.
Compare the job with the drawing; report and put right any error before the parts are joined or welded to anything else.

blocks.p: Any error in the pattern is carried into the job. A cylinder pattern a few millimetres short will not close; one too long overlaps and the diameter is wrong. Parts that do not fit must be made again, wasting steel, time and money. Check the drawing and your sums twice, make a card trial where you can, and check the marked sheet before you cut.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can handle sheet, snips, scribers, guillotines and rolls safely.
I can choose and use the marking-out tools, and explain why bend lines are marked in pencil.
I can mark out from a straight datum edge.
I can name the lines, angles, triangles, polygons, parts of a circle and solids used in fabrication.
I can state the angle sums of a triangle (180°) and a four-sided shape (360°).
I can work out circumference, mean diameter, stretch-out, duct perimeter, box sheet size and the number of pieces from a sheet.
I can work out a slant height, a cone sector angle and a true length.
I can bisect a line and an angle, and construct 90°, 60°, 45°, 30° and parallel lines.
I can construct an equilateral triangle, a hexagon, and an octagon in a square, divide a circle into 12, and find a lost centre.
I can draw an elevation and plan and find the true length of a sloping line.
I can develop a cylinder and a pipe cut at an angle by the parallel line method.
I can develop a cone, a frustum and a square pyramid by the radial line method.
I can add lap, seam, wired edge, safe edge and flange allowances.
I can transfer a pattern to sheet, cut, deburr and form it, and check the finished job.

c1.title: A hood for a jerk pan in Boston, Portland
c1.text: A jerk centre in Boston, Portland, wants a sheet-steel hood in the shape of a cone frustum to sit over a jerk pan and lead the smoke into a flue. The drawing gives a bottom diameter of 800 mm, a top diameter of 400 mm and a vertical height of 150 mm. Nadine, a Level 2 trainee, is to develop the pattern.

c2.title: An extractor duct for a bakery in Black River
c2.text: A bakery in Black River, St Elizabeth, needs a round extractor duct of 250 mm diameter in 0.8 mm galvanised sheet, with a 10 mm lap allowance for the riveted seam. Where it passes through the sloping roof, the duct must be cut off at 45°, with its shortest side 200 mm long. Garfield is drawing the pattern, dividing the plan into 12.

c3.title: A water-tank shell in Lucea
c3.text: A fabrication shop in Lucea, Hanover, is rolling the shell of a small water tank from 5 mm mild steel plate. The drawing gives an inside diameter of 450 mm and a height of 900 mm, and the seam is to be butt welded, with no lap. Kevin, the trainee, wants to work out the plate length from 460 mm, "the outside, because that is what you measure".

c4.title: Base plates for a gazebo in Annotto Bay
c4.text: At a training centre in Annotto Bay, St Mary, a group is marking out base plates for the posts of a steel gazebo. Some plates are regular hexagons with 80 mm sides; others are regular octagons marked inside 100 mm squares. The plates are marked on 6 mm plate with dividers, a rule and a scriber.

c5.title: A tray for a fruit cart in Bog Walk
c5.text: Tamika is making open-top trays for a fruit vendor's cart in Bog Walk, St Catherine. Each tray is 400 mm long, 250 mm wide and 60 mm deep, folded from one piece of 1 mm sheet. The shop buys sheets of 2 440 mm × 1 220 mm. Tabs will be added to the corners so they can be lapped and riveted.

questions.q: Why must Nadine extend the two sloping sides upward until they meet?
o: To find the apex, which is the centre for both arcs
To check that the hood will be tall enough for the flue
To find the length of the seam that will be welded
To find where the top of the hood should be cut off
questions.why: The frustum pattern is part of the pattern for the full cone. Both arcs are struck from the full cone's apex, which is found by extending the sloping sides until they meet.

questions.q: The full cone is 300 mm high with a base radius of 400 mm. What is the radius of the outer arc of the pattern?
questions.why: The outer arc's radius is the slant height of the full cone: √(400² + 300²) = √250 000 = 500 mm. The 400 mm and 300 mm are the base radius and the vertical height, not slant lengths.

questions.q: What is the sector angle of Nadine's pattern?
questions.why: Sector angle = base radius ÷ slant height × 360° = 400 ÷ 500 × 360° = 288°. The pattern is a large sector, more than three-quarters of a circle.

questions.q: How long must the outer curved edge of the pattern be, without allowances? (Take π as 3.142.)
questions.why: The outer edge forms the bottom of the hood, so it equals the base circumference: 3.142 × 800 = 2 513.6 mm. 1 256.8 mm uses the top diameter, and 5 027.2 mm doubles the circumference.

questions.q: How long is Garfield's pattern from end to end, including the lap? (Take π as 3.142.)
questions.why: Stretch-out = 3.142 × 250 = 785.5 mm. The lap allowance goes on one end only, giving 785.5 + 10 = 795.5 mm.

questions.q: The shortest side is 200 mm and the cut is at 45°. How long is the longest side of the duct?
questions.why: A cut at 45° rises by the same distance as it goes across, so across a 250 mm duct it rises 250 mm: 200 + 250 = 450 mm.

questions.q: How wide is each of the 12 spaces on Garfield's stretch-out line?
questions.why: The stretch-out is 785.5 mm (without the lap), so each space is 785.5 ÷ 12 = 65.5 mm. 20.8 mm is the diameter divided by 12, and 66.3 mm wrongly includes the lap.

questions.q: Which diameter should the plate length be worked out from?
questions.why: The length is set by the middle of the plate thickness. With an inside diameter of 450 mm and 5 mm plate, the mean diameter is 450 + 5 = 455 mm.

questions.q: What length of plate is needed for the shell? (Take π as 3.142.)
questions.why: Length = π × mean diameter = 3.142 × 455 = 1 429.6 mm, by 900 mm high. 1 413.9 mm uses the inside diameter and 1 445.3 mm the outside.

questions.q: If Kevin works the length from 460 mm, what will happen when the plate is rolled?
o: The edges will not meet, leaving a gap of about 16 mm
The plate will be about 16 mm too long, so it overlaps
Nothing, as 10 mm on the diameter makes no real difference
The shell will come out oval instead of truly round
questions.why: From 460 mm the plate is 3.142 × 460 = 1 445.3 mm, about 15.7 mm longer than needed. The edges overlap instead of meeting for the butt weld, or the tank comes out oversize.

questions.q: What is the distance across the corners of one hexagon plate?
questions.why: A regular hexagon's side equals the radius of the circle round it, so the distance across the corners is the diameter: 2 × 80 = 160 mm. About 139 mm is the distance across the flats.

questions.q: For an octagon in a 100 mm square, what radius is swung from each corner?
o: 50 mm, half the side length of the square
70.7 mm, half the diagonal of the square
100 mm, the full side length of the square
41.4 mm, the length of each octagon side
questions.why: Each arc is struck from a corner through the centre of the square, so its radius is half the diagonal: √(100² + 100²) ÷ 2 = 70.7 mm. The arcs cut the sides at the octagon's corners.

questions.q: A trainee checks the octagon plates with a protractor. What should each inside angle measure?
questions.why: The inside angles of an 8-sided shape add up to (8 − 2) × 180° = 1 080°, so each of the eight equal angles is 135°. 120° belongs to a hexagon and 108° to a pentagon.

questions.q: Before the corner tabs are added, what is cut out of each corner of the flat blank?
o: Nothing: the corners are folded in
questions.why: Each side is folded up 60 mm, so a square equal to the depth, 60 mm × 60 mm, comes out of each corner of the 520 mm × 370 mm blank. Tabs for the lapped corners are added to this outline.

questions.q: Ignoring allowances and cutting waste, how many 520 mm × 370 mm blanks can be cut from one 2 440 mm × 1 220 mm sheet?
questions.why: 2 440 ÷ 520 = 4 whole pieces and 1 220 ÷ 370 = 3, giving 12. Turned the other way, 2 440 ÷ 370 = 6 and 1 220 ÷ 520 = 2, also 12. Only whole pieces count.

questions.q: The corners are to be lapped and riveted. What must be added to the pattern?
o: Nothing, as rivets need no extra metal
Extra length on every side of the tray
A wired edge round the whole top of the tray
A tab at each corner, as wide as the lap
questions.why: A lapped joint needs metal that overlaps the neighbouring side, so a lap tab is added at each corner. Leaving it off means there is nothing to rivet through.

questions.q: A square pyramid has base sides of 200 mm and a vertical height of 300 mm. What is the true length of each sloping corner edge, to the nearest millimetre?
questions.why: The plan length of a corner edge is half the base diagonal, 141.4 mm. True length = √(141.4² + 300²) = √110 000 = 331.7 mm, about 332 mm.

questions.q: Anthony must divide a 170 mm line into 7 equal parts with dividers and a straight edge. Which method works?
o: Step 24 mm along it seven times and trim off whatever is left
Bisect it, then bisect each half, then bisect each quarter again
Step 7 spaces on a sloping line, join the last, draw parallels
Draw a circle on it and step its radius round it seven times
questions.why: Stepping equal spaces along a sloping line, joining the last mark to the end of the line and drawing parallels through the other marks divides the line exactly into 7, whatever its length. Bisecting only gives 2, 4 or 8 parts.

questions.q: Why does stepping 12 equal divider spaces round a cone pattern's arc make the pattern a little short?
o: Each step is a straight chord, shorter than its arc
The dividers close up slightly each time they are lifted
The arc is always drawn with a radius that is too small
The plan circle should be divided into 13 parts, not 12
questions.why: A divider step measures the straight chord, which is slightly shorter than the curved arc it spans; twelve steps come out about 1% short. More divisions, or the calculated sector angle, are more accurate.

questions.q: What does each inside angle of a regular pentagon measure?
questions.why: The inside angles of a 5-sided shape add up to (5 − 2) × 180° = 540°, so each of five equal angles is 108°. 72° is the angle at the centre between two corners.
